articles.title: What is in my Two Engines Kit for Claude Code and Codex, and the numbers behind each part
articles.excerpt: If you use Claude Code and Codex on the same projects, you probably keep two rule files, review by hand and push more often than you want to. The Two Engines Kit is the set of files I run both engines…
articles.body: If you use Claude Code and Codex on the same projects, you probably keep two rule files, review by hand and push more often than you want to. The Two Engines Kit is the set of files I run both engines with, packed so one script installs them. I've been building it since the first Codex and Claude CLIs, and every number below comes from my own logs on my own projects. This post walks through each part, what it does and the measurement that made me add it. Who does what In my setup Claude Code writes and Codex reviews. An orchestrator session in Claude Code plans the work, writes the briefs, starts workers in their own git worktrees, reads their diffs, runs the local gate and merges. Workers never push.

articles.title: One-pass Hopalong orbit density plot
articles.excerpt: This script renders the classic Hopalong map as a visit-density image. It The goal is to plot a long orbit with: Memory bounded by the histogram dimensions, rather than the number of iterations. Exact…
articles.body: This script renders the classic Hopalong map as a visit-density image. It streams the orbit into a fixed-size histogram and adapts the represented coordinate range when necessary, rather than storing every orbit point or making a full preliminary pass to discover the bounds. Target The goal is to plot a long orbit with: Memory bounded by the histogram dimensions, rather than the number of iterations. Exact integer visit counts at the histogram's final cell resolution. Automatic coverage when the orbit moves beyond the current grid, at the finest cell size that still fits the whole orbit. A useful density visualization, optionally Gaussian-smoothed. The implementation uses NumPy arrays, Matplotlib, and Numba.

articles.excerpt: A mismatch before the first sentence An English voice bundle attached to a Russian request is a problem before the first sentence exists. The request can be well formed while carrying writing instruct…
articles.body: A mismatch before the first sentence An English voice bundle attached to a Russian request is a problem before the first sentence exists. The request can be well formed while carrying writing instructions that belong to a different language or format. I want to catch that mismatch while the input is still something I can inspect. In Quillgrain , I compile an explicitly chosen voice pack into local writing context, then verify that context before handing it to a model. That gives me a concrete boundary in a writing tool: prepare the instructions, check their identity and scope, then ask for prose. Compilation itself does not call Ollama or any other model.

When Censys reported 2,991 internet-exposed Danfoss StoreView control panels on 11 October 2026 and a ZoomEye header query returned 260 global assets on 22 October 2026, the reflex is to ask which one is right. The more useful question is what each instrument was built to see. The two observations, stated precisely Censys described a scan performed against its own telemetry on 11 October 2026, the day a cyber-attack hit cooling systems at hundreds of French supermarkets. It counted 2,991 hosts with a Danfoss StoreView control panel, 1,825 of them, or 61%, in France.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

articles.title: Medusa's eye, Halloween fireballs and more: 5 skywatching targets to look out for this spooky season
articles.excerpt: Five spooky skywatching targets perfect for naked eye stargazing this Halloween!
articles.body: The spooky season is officially here! To celebrate, we've put together a list of five Halloween-themed skywatching targets that you can enjoy with nothing but the naked eye or binoculars and, of course, clear skies. Over millennia, the night sky has helped shape human beliefs. In return, we have imprinted our myths, stories and perceptions upon it, seeing monsters and mythology in the twinkling lights of the stars and assigning sinister aspects to innocent cosmic objects. Many of these ghostly impressions and meanings have survived to the present day. Here are a few of our favorites. The Pleiades open star cluster Don't be fooled by their beauty; the blue-white stars of the Pleiades are dripping in spooky lore.

At the time the comet-chasing spacecraft was about 472 million kilometers from planet Earth, but only 16 kilometers from the surface of comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko .
